docs.title: Biotope
docs.text:
Biotope is a framework that helps your AI agents build and maintain purpose-driven knowledge representations. Imagine you need to build a knowledge graph that uses messy clinical data to find promising drug targets, or maintain a database of all people, events, and resources of a distributed organization. You can give raw data and the purpose statement to the biotope agent and it will build the graph topology, mapping, entity and conflict resolution, following the industry best practices. Biotope simplifies the process of building and maintaining the data project, but semantic authority and final decisions on the representation stays with the human.

How data projects that are created by the biotope agent work:

  • Inputs. Structured files are described automatically using croissant-baker: CSV, TSV, Excel, Parquet, JSON, HDF5 and AnnData, FHIR, VCF, BAM, FASTA, DICOM, NIfTI, images and more. Unstructured documents, such as papers and web pages, become records through an extractor the agent writes, and each value keeps the quote it came from.
  • Output. Neo4j import files or one SQLite file. Every node and edge names the source rows it came from.
  • Maintainability. The biotope-created data project is plain Python in a fixed layout and static type-checking for all entities and mappings. New data of the same shape rebuilds with commands only, and a change in the data's structure is reported before the build.
  • Versioning. Everything Biotope writes is a plain file that you commit with your own git. Each build records its code, data revisions and library versions.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Get started: install the plugin and start a project.
  • Working with the agent: the purpose statement, your decisions and the review.
  • Use the result: load the graph into Neo4j, query it in SQLite and trace its values.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Biotope does not decide which records are the same thing. You or the agent decide, and the agent records the decision.
  • The checks test the structure of the graph. Review its content against the sources.
  • The whole graph is held in memory during a build, so choose a scope that fits the machine.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: Biotope follows semantic versioning: a change that breaks your project comes in a new major version. The changelog lists the changes in each release.

docs.title: Working with the agent
docs.text: You decide what the graph is for and make the choices that change its answers. The agent describes the data, writes and runs the code, and reports what it did.

docs.title: Write the purpose statement
docs.text:
The purpose statement says who uses the graph, for which tasks, and the typical questions they ask. The agent drafts it from your first message and a first look at the data. You correct the draft, and the agent records it with biotope map --purpose. The node and edge types follow from the questions, and the agent checks later choices against them. The agent will interview you and will try to align on the purpose by asking.

Example for organization management: "Institute staff and management use the graph to find who works on what. Typical questions: which groups work on single-cell methods? Who has published with a given partner institute? Which research will be most suited for this upcoming grant?"

For biomedical research: "The target-discovery team ranks genes as drug targets for liver fibrosis. Typical questions: which genes change expression in fibrotic tissue in at least two studies? Which of them have a known compound?"

docs.title: What you get back
docs.text:
• The graph in graph/build/. Use the result explains each file.
  • A hand-over report: the sources selected and excluded, with reasons; the records excluded, per rule; the claims the agent checked against the sources; and the open questions.
  • graph/ASSUMPTIONS.md, with the decisions and the open questions.

docs.title: Review the result
docs.text:
Biotope's checks test the structure of the graph. However, agents are not very good in understanding semantics of the relations and can sometimes make trivial mistakes. Biotope enforces best practices, and makes it hard for an agent to make technical mistaked, but always check if the final representation is sensible:

  1. Read the hand-over report and graph/ASSUMPTIONS.md.
  2. Check if the questions that the biotope agent generated from the purpose and used for testing the graph are representative.
  3. Open the metagraph viewer and check that the node and edge types can answer your questions.
  4. Pick a few values you know and trace them to their sources.

docs.title: Later
docs.text: When new data of the same shape arrives, ask the agent to update the graph. A change in the data's structure, such as a new column or a new table, needs the agent.

docs.title: Miscellaneous
docs.text: • release 1.0.0 (14235dc)

docs.title: ⚠ BREAKING CHANGES
docs.text:
• graph: project validation callbacks and per-capability states are gone, so builds no longer verify scientific expectations; structural checks are not equivalent, and review-time independent reads replace them. interpretation no longer travels inside the graph; concept and property descriptions in schema_config.yaml, run.json policies and scope, and graph/ASSUMPTIONS.md replace the query context, so graph/build/ must travel with the graph. biotope graph quality prints its results instead of writing graph/reports/quality.json; biotope graph metagraph writes graph/metagraph.html by default. schemas are never re-rendered. Generated and 0.9 schemas no longer follow manifest changes; each change surfaces as source.drift for review. Authored types are not compared with Croissant dataType or nullability. new scaffolds bind fields through @ids scoped under their RecordSet; other ids produce source.unscoped_field, while an existing __field_refs__ mapping still binds them. a new package's name depends on the directories that already exist, so it can differ from a from-scratch generation. removed keywords such as SourceContract(generated=) and Pipeline(query_context=) fail with ordinary TypeErrors; run.json and definition reports are schema_version 2 (replacement and --report accept 1 and 2). See docs/migration.md for the 0.9 migration steps.
  • graph: builds no longer write topology.json, ontology.ttl, query_context.json, provenance.jsonl or BiotopeQueryContext rows. Provenance is reached through each object's biotope_provenance_id in provenance.json. biotope graph build defaults to <graph>/build and replaces the previous generated build instead of requiring a new --out directory; --out still chooses another location. Export is headless and labels drop the namespace (for example Gene rather than CvdGene), so Entity is no longer reserved.

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text: Run each command from the project folder as uv run --project graph biotope …. Commands that write a report take --json and then write one JSON document to stdout.

docs.title: biotope
docs.text:
Biotope is a framework that helps AI agents build and maintain purpose-driven knowledge representations.

Usage:

biotope [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

Options:

Name Type Description Default --version boolean Show the version and exit. False --help boolean Show this message and exit. False

Subcommands

  • add: Describe data files or folders as datasets, and create the annotation file of each.
  • annotate: Write what people know about a dataset into its annotation file, and validate descriptions.
  • check-data: Compare the data files with the SHA-256 checksums their descriptions record, and report each changed file.
  • config: Manage the project metadata that biotope add applies to every dataset.
  • extract: Extract records from documents with the extractions listed in graph/extraction.
  • graph: Scaffold, check, assess, visualize or build one graph workspace.
  • init: Create a Biotope project in the folder NAME, or in the current folder with NAME ".".
  • map: Record the project's purpose and inspect Croissant metadata.
  • mark: Set the biotope:status of DATASET to STATUS.
  • mv: Move a tracked file or directory and update every description and source package that names it.
  • queue: Show every dataset grouped by its status: raw, processed or mapped.
  • rm: Remove a dataset or a file from Biotope, with its data unless --keep-data is given.
  • source: Register authored descriptions and scaffold project-owned source packages.
  • status: List the dataset manifests in .biotope/datasets and mark those whose revision differs from the one their source package in graph/sources pins.

docs.title: add
docs.text:
Describe data files or folders as datasets, and create the annotation file of each.

Usage:

biotope add [OPTIONS] [PATHS]...

Options:

Name Type Description Default --rebake boolean Describe an already-tracked dataset again from its data and annotation file False --json boolean Emit a complete machine-readable scan report on stdout False --name text Dataset name override None --description text Dataset description override None --license text Dataset license None --creator text Dataset creator name None --creator-email text Dataset creator email None --url text Dataset URL None --citation text Dataset citation text None --version text Dataset version None --keyword text Dataset keyword (repeatable) None --access-restrictions text Dataset access restrictions None --legal-obligations text Dataset legal obligations None --collaboration-partner text Dataset collaboration partner None --rai text Croissant RAI field as KEY=VALUE None --status choice (raw | processed) Override workflow state. Default: 'processed' when fields are described, 'raw' otherwise. This does not validate values. None --derived-from text Record this dataset as derived from another (repeatable). Pass a dataset reference — data path, manifest path, or dataset name. None --help boolean Show this message and exit. False

docs.title: annotate
docs.text:
Write what people know about a dataset into its annotation file, and validate descriptions.

Usage:

biotope annotate [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

Options:

Name Type Description Default --help boolean Show this message and exit. False

Subcommands

  • set: Write KEY=VALUE pairs into the annotation file of DATA, a dataset biotope add described.
  • validate: Validate a Croissant metadata file.

docs.title: set
docs.text:
Write KEY=VALUE pairs into the annotation file of DATA, a dataset biotope add described.

Without --table the values describe the dataset, with --table that table, and with --column that column. A repeated KEY makes a list, and an empty VALUE clears what the data says. A table's key names its columns, as in key=person_id; an equivalent property is a URL, as in equivalentProperty=https://schema.org/name.

Usage:

biotope annotate set [OPTIONS] DATA VALUES...

Options:

Name Type Description Default --table text A table's ID as biotope map inspect prints it, such as push/people.csv#people. None --column text A column of --table, by its name in the data. None --help boolean Show this message and exit. False

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
Validate a Croissant metadata file.

Usage:

biotope annotate validate [OPTIONS]

Options:

docs.title: Documents
docs.text:
Papers, web pages, contracts and other unstructured documents become structured records through extraction. The agent writes one extractor for each kind of document. Biotope runs it, keeps the quote or location behind each value, and stores the records as a dataset that the graph reads like any table.

After the extraction, the document will be treated like just another structured document and will become part of the knowledge representation through standard topology mapping.

docs.title: What you decide
docs.text:
• Which services may read the documents, such as a model API, and how API keys are supplied. The agent asks before it sends a document to an external service. You need to provide keys and LLM endpoints to the agent.
  • What to extract. The agent proposes a schema: the kind of record, its fields, and the question each field serves. It runs the schema on a few sample documents and shows you each value with its quote. It extracts all documents after you approve, and asks again after each change to the schema.

docs.title: The commands
docs.text:
uv run --project graph biotope extract try papers data/papers/smith2024.pdf
uv run --project graph biotope extract run
uv run --project graph biotope extract run papers --redo data/papers/smith2024.pdf
  • extract try NAME FILE... runs one extraction on the given files and shows the records with their evidence. It changes nothing.
  • extract run runs every extraction, or the ones you name, and stores the records.
  • --redo FILE extracts that document again.

docs.title: Where the records are
docs.text:
Each extraction stores its records in data/extracted/<name>.jsonl, one record per line. Each value keeps its quote or location, and each record names its document, the schema revision and the extractor:

{
  "id": "calls/call.md#round=\"Full proposal\"",
  "document": "data/calls/call.md",
  "values": {
    "deadline": {"value": "30 April 2027", "evidence": {"quote": "| Full proposal | 30 April 2027 |", "locator": null}}
  },
  "provenance": {
    "document_sha256": "0e2faf46…",
    "schema": "FundingRound",
    "schema_revision": "065fb9fb…",
    "extractor": {"name": "round-reader", "version": "1", "settings": {}}
  }
}

docs.title: When a document is extracted again
docs.text: A run extracts a document only when it is new or changed, or when the schema or the extractor changed. Otherwise it reuses the stored records. Extraction usually calls a paid model, so a change to the schema means model calls for every document. An interrupted run can be started again: it reuses the documents it finished.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text: You should use Biotope through a coding agent. You give it the data and the purpose of the graph. The agent describes the data, writes and runs the project's code, and asks you about the choices that change the graph's answers.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Install uv and Claude Code. uv installs Python 3.10, 3.11 or 3.12 for the project when needed.
  • Choose the project folder: your repository, or a new folder. Put the data in it, for example under data/.
  • Keep each dataset at a fixed path. A file's ID in Biotope is its path, so a dataset saved to a new folder on each download gets new IDs, and the agent has to update the project.

docs.title: Install the plugin
docs.text:
In Claude Code (or any other agent harness), add the Biotope marketplace and install the plugin:

/plugin marketplace add biocypher/biotope#biotope-v1.0.0
/plugin install biotope@biotope

Install it for your user to use it in every project. To check it, type / in Claude Code: /biotope:biotope-croissant is in the list.

docs.title: Start a project
docs.text:
Start Claude Code with claude in the project folder. Tell it where the data is and what the graph is for. For an organization:

Use biotope to build a knowledge graph from the files in data/. It is for our institute's staff, who look up who works on which topic, in which group and on which projects.

Example, for a biomedical project:

Use biotope to build a knowledge graph from the clinical tables and papers in data/. It is for our target-discovery team, who rank genes by the evidence that links them to liver fibrosis.

The agent then installs Biotope into an environment for the project:

  • graph/pyproject.toml lists Biotope and the libraries that the project's code reads data with, and graph/uv.lock pins their versions. Commit both.
  • Every command runs as uv run --project graph biotope … from the project folder. Use the same form when you run a command yourself.

Working with the agent describes what happens next.

docs.title: Other agents
docs.text: Cursor and Codex use the same skill. Copy the folder skills/biotope-croissant from the Biotope repository into your project's .cursor/skills/ for Cursor or .agents/skills/ for Codex.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
• Croissant: a standard format for describing datasets: their files, tables and fields.
  • croissant-baker: the tool that reads your data files and writes their Croissant description. Describing a dataset again after its data changed is a rebake.
  • Manifest: the Croissant description of one dataset, in .biotope/datasets/. Biotope writes it from the data and the annotation file.
  • Annotation file: the file next to a dataset, .biotope.yaml, where people and the agent write what they know about it, such as descriptions, keys, the creator and the license.
  • Table: the rows of one file, or of one sheet or part of a file. Croissant calls it a record set.
  • Structured file: a file that code can read into records, such as a CSV, Excel or Parquet file.
  • Unstructured document: a file that needs reading, such as a paper or a web page. Extraction turns it into records.
  • Graph workspace: the graph/ folder, which holds the project's code and its builds.
  • Source package: the Python folder in graph/sources/ that reads one table or file into typed records.
  • Source revision: a fingerprint of a source's structure: its fields, types and keys. When the structure changes, the check reports drift.
  • Topology: the node and edge types of the graph, with their properties and descriptions.
  • Alignment: deciding which records from different sources are the same thing.
  • Mapping: a function that turns typed records into nodes and edges.
  • Provenance: the source rows behind each node and edge.
  • Run record: run.json, what one build read, selected, excluded and wrote.
  • BioCypher: the framework that writes the Neo4j import files.

docs.title: Your project
docs.text: Biotope keeps its state in plain files in your project folder. This page says what to commit, where to write what you know about a dataset, and how to rebuild the graph when new data arrives. Run each command from the project folder.

docs.title: What Biotope writes
docs.text:
Commit these files and folders with the rest of the project:

  • .biotope/: the project's purpose, the creator and license that apply to every dataset, and the manifests.
  • graph/: the graph workspace, with the project's code, graph/pyproject.toml and graph/uv.lock. Git ignores the build in graph/build/ and the viewer graph/metagraph.html.
  • data/extracted/: the records extracted from documents.
  • The annotation file next to each dataset.

Biotope does not run git. When git would ignore a file that you must commit, Biotope warns you.

When the project has no .gitignore, Biotope writes one. It keeps the data files under data/ out of git, and keeps the annotation files and extracted records in:

/data/**
!/data/**/
!/data/**/*.biotope.yaml
!/data/extracted/**
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.venv/
.env

If your .gitignore has a /data/ or data/ rule, replace that rule with the first four lines above. Git cannot keep a file whose folder it ignores.

docs.title: The annotation file
docs.text:
Each dataset has an annotation file, where people and the agent write what they know about it: data/study/.biotope.yaml for the folder data/study, and data/raw/samples.csv.biotope.yaml for the single file data/raw/samples.csv.

description: People and reports of one synthetic study.
license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
creator: Ada Lovelace
tables:
  push/people.csv#people:
    description: One row per person.
    key: person_id
    columns:
      person_id:
        description: The person's ID in the study's export.

A value in the file replaces what croissant-baker reads from the data, a missing value comes from the data, and an empty value clears it. Edit the file by hand, or ask the agent. Do not edit the manifest in .biotope/datasets/: Biotope makes it from the data and this file.

docs.title: IDs come from paths
docs.text:
Each file's ID is its path within its dataset, such as push/people.csv, and each table's ID is its file's ID and its name, such as push/people.csv#people. New data with the same paths keeps every ID, and the project's code keeps working. Keep each dataset at a fixed path. To move a file, use biotope mv, which updates every ID that points to it:

uv run --project graph biotope mv data/study/push/people.csv data/study/current/people.csv

docs.title: New data
docs.text:
When new data of the same shape arrives, such as new rows, a new file or a newer download of a document, rebuild with these commands:

uv run --project graph biotope add --rebake data/study
uv run --project graph biotope extract run
uv run --project graph biotope source generate .biotope/datasets/data/study.jsonld --out graph/sources
uv run --project graph biotope graph check
uv run --project graph biotope graph build
  • Run add --rebake and source generate once per changed dataset.
  • Run extract run when the project extracts records from documents. It extracts only the new and changed documents.

Two changes need the agent:

  • A new table or file gets a new source package that does not read anything yet. graph check fails until the agent writes the package or excludes it with a reason. When the graph must rebuild without anyone at hand, ask the agent to exclude new inputs by default.
  • A change in structure, such as a new column, a changed column type or a new key, makes graph check report drift. The agent reviews the change and updates the code. A changed description does not cause drift.

docs.title: Check the state
docs.text:
• uv run --project graph biotope status lists the manifests and marks each one whose structure changed since its source packages were written.
  • uv run --project graph biotope check-data compares the data files with the checksums Biotope recorded, and reports each changed file.
  • The CLI reference lists every command.

docs.title: Use the result
docs.text: Each build writes the graph and the files that explain it to graph/build/. Share these files with the graph: the meaning of each value is in schema_config.yaml, and its source is in provenance.json.

docs.title: What a build writes
docs.text:
• biocypher/: the graph as Neo4j import files, a header and a data file per node and edge type, and the import script neo4j-admin-import-call.sh.
  • graph.sqlite: the graph as one SQLite file, instead of biocypher/, when the build ran with --format sqlite.
  • schema_config.yaml: every node and edge type with its properties and their descriptions.
  • provenance.json: the source rows behind every node and edge.
  • run.json: the run record, with the purpose, the selected and excluded sources, the excluded records per rule, the counts, and the versions of the code, data and libraries.

A build replaces graph/build/ only when it succeeds. A failed build keeps the previous graph and writes graph/build/last_failure.json.

docs.title: Load the graph into Neo4j
docs.text:
Stop a running Neo4j database (if present), then run the import script from the Neo4j installation folder:

cd /path/to/neo4j
bash /path/to/project/graph/build/biocypher/neo4j-admin-import-call.sh

The script replaces the database neo4j with the graph. Start Neo4j again and query it with Cypher. The Neo4j manual describes the import tool.

docs.title: Query the SQLite file
docs.text:
Ask the agent to build with --format sqlite, or run uv run --project graph biotope graph build --format sqlite. Each node and edge type is a table, and each edge table has source and target columns that reference node tables. In the tutorial graph, this lists each airline at SFO with its role:

SELECT Airline.name, AirlineRoleAtAirport.role
FROM AirlineRoleAtAirport
JOIN Airline ON Airline.id = AirlineRoleAtAirport.source
WHERE AirlineRoleAtAirport.target = 'airport:SFO';

docs.title: View the topology
docs.text:
The metagraph viewer shows the node and edge types with their descriptions and the counts from a build:

uv run --project graph biotope graph metagraph --report graph/build/run.json

Open graph/metagraph.html in a browser. It works offline.

docs.title: Trace a value to its source
docs.text:
• Every node and edge has a biotope_provenance_id, a position in the records list of provenance.json. That record names the mappings that made it and its evidence: each source file, its version and the row or page.
  • run.json lists the excluded sources with their reasons under definitions.excluded_sources, and the excluded records under findings, one entry per rule with a count and sample rows.

docs.title: Tutorial: explore a finished project
docs.text: This tutorial explores a small finished project: six airports, five airlines, and the notes an operations desk keeps on them. The graph shows which airline uses which airport as a hub or a focus city. You see what an agent leaves in a project, then check and build it yourself. You write no code. You need uv and git.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
Copy the example from the Biotope release and install its environment:

git clone --depth 1 --branch biotope-v1.0.0 https://github.com/biocypher/biotope.git

cp -R biotope/examples/airports my-airports
cd my-airports
uv sync --project graph

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
The project has two kinds of data:

  • data/airports/ holds three CSV tables: the airports, the airlines, and which airline has a hub at which airport.
  • data/notes/airport-notes.md holds the desk's notes, one section per airport. Each section states its roles in sentences such as "Hub for Delta Air Lines." and "Focus city for Alaska Airlines."

The two sources disagree once. hubs.csv lists Alaska Airlines as a hub at SFO, and the notes call SFO a focus city for Alaska Airlines.

docs.title: Read the project
docs.text:
The agent agreed the purpose with the desk, described the data, wrote an extractor for the notes and asked how to resolve the disagreement. These files hold the result:

  • .biotope/project.yaml holds the purpose and its typical questions.
  • data/.biotope.yaml describes each table and column.
  • graph/extraction/airport_notes.py declares the record the notes yield and reads them with regular expressions. The notes are internal, so no model reads them.
  • graph/ASSUMPTIONS.md lists the questions the agent asked and the desk's answers.
  • graph/alignment/airlines.py matches the airline names in the notes to the codes in airlines.csv.
  • graph/mappings/role.py takes each role from the notes and leaves out the row of hubs.csv they contradict.

docs.title: Extract from the notes
docs.text:
uv run --project graph biotope extract try airport_role_claims data/notes/airport-notes.md

The output lists 12 records, each with the sentence and the line it comes from. Nothing in the project changes. The agent stored the same records with biotope extract run in data/extracted/airport_role_claims.jsonl, and the graph reads them from there.

docs.title: Check and build
docs.text:
uv run --project graph biotope graph check
uv run --project graph biotope graph build

The build also prints BioCypher's log lines and, on the first run, warnings from the rdflib library. You can ignore both. The build writes 11 nodes and 12 edges to graph/build/: the six airports, the five airlines, and one edge for each role an airline has at an airport. graph/build/run.json lists one excluded record under the rule hub_row_superseded_by_notes: line 13 of hubs.csv, where Alaska Airlines is a hub at SFO. Use the result explains each file the build writes.

docs.title: View the topology
docs.text:
uv run --project graph biotope graph metagraph --report graph/build/run.json

Open graph/metagraph.html in a browser to see the node and edge types with their descriptions and counts.

docs.title: Build it with the agent
docs.text:
To see how an agent arrives at such a project, give it the raw data in a new folder:

mkdir -p ../my-own/data
cp -R data/airports data/notes ../my-own/data/

Start Claude Code in my-own and use the example's purpose:

Use biotope to build a knowledge graph from the files in data/. Purpose: our operations team looks up which airlines use which airports as hubs or focus cities. Typical questions: which airlines have a hub at JFK? Where does United have hubs? Which airports are a focus city, and for which airline? The notes are internal, so extract from them with code, not with a model.

The sources leave open which of them is right about SFO and how a name in the notes matches an airline code, so expect the agent to ask. Compare its node and edge types and its exclusions with this example.
